---
title: "Multiple Imputation in All-In-One Mediation"
output: html_document
---

## Impute and analyze in one call

Use `missing = "mi"`. When omitted, `fit_method` automatically becomes
`"sem"` and `R` becomes 20000 for MI. Other missing-data methods retain
their existing defaults. Explicit regression fitting is rejected. For a raw data frame,
the function calls `mice`, fits the automatically generated path model
with `lavaan.mi`, and computes Monte Carlo confidence intervals.
The following data are artificial; this is an interface illustration,
not evidence of comparative method performance.

```{r}
library(manymome)
set.seed(317)
n <- 200
x <- rnorm(n)
c1 <- rnorm(n)
z <- rnorm(n)
m <- 0.5*x + 0.3*c1 + 0.4*z + rnorm(n)
y <- 0.2*x + 0.4*m + 0.2*c1 + rnorm(n)
dat <- data.frame(x, m, y, c1, z)
dat$m[runif(n) < plogis(-1 + 0.5*z)] <- NA

out <- q_simple_mediation(
  x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", cov = "c1", data = dat,
  fit_method = "sem", missing = "mi",
  mi_vars = "z", mice_args = list(m = 20, maxit = 10),
  mi_seed = 123, ci_type = "mc", R = 2000, seed = 456,
  parallel = FALSE, progress = FALSE
)
print(out, pvalue = FALSE)
```

Use more Monte Carlo draws when greater precision is needed. The two seeds
make imputation and interval generation reproducible separately. If no
imputation seed is specified, `seed` is also used for imputation.

The imputation data contain the modeled variables and `z`. Extra columns
in the original data, such as IDs, are not included automatically.
`z` is used only for imputation: it does not become a control variable in
the mediation equations. Use `cov` to adjust those equations.

## Inspect imputation and fitting

```{r}
out$mi_info
out$imputation$loggedEvents
head(out$imputed_data[[1]])
fit <- get_fit(out)
```

The `mids` object in `out$imputation` retains convergence/chain information
and imputation settings. Inspect it using the diagnostic tools in `mice`.
Default settings (including 20 imputations) are starting settings, not a
guarantee of adequate convergence, sufficient imputation count, or MAR.
Customize `mice_args` with appropriate methods, predictor matrices and
iterations based on the data and scientific model.

## Reuse existing imputations

```{r}
out_existing <- q_simple_mediation(
  x = "x", m = "m", y = "y", cov = "c1",
  data = out$imputation,
  fit_method = "sem", missing = "mi", ci_type = "mc",
  R = 2000, seed = 456, parallel = FALSE, progress = FALSE
)
# Equivalently, supply data = out$imputed_data.
```

Do not set `mice_args`, `mi_vars` or `mi_seed` when supplying existing
imputations; these settings apply only when imputing raw data.
At least two usable imputations are required. Every completed data frame
must have complete numeric modeled variables and the same number of cases.
Omissions for nonconvergence or unavailable SEs are reported.

## Initial scope and interpretation

Simple, serial, parallel and custom observed-variable linear models are
supported. Numeric binary predictors are allowed. Indicators, moderators,
categorical modeled variables, grouped, clustered and weighted analyses
are not yet supported by this interface. Numeric model variables are
checked, but scientific model assumptions still need assessment.

MI defaults to Monte Carlo confidence intervals. Explicit bootstrap
requests raise an error. `boot_ci = FALSE, mc_ci = FALSE` requests point
estimates without indirect-effect intervals.
Pooled path estimates use Rubin pooling as implemented by `lavaan.mi`.
Raw and standardized indirect/direct effects use manymome's existing
post-fitting MI methods. Pooled standardized path tables, R-square tests
and quick plots are not yet provided; they are not replaced by results
from an arbitrarily selected imputation. `get_fit()` provides the fitted
MI object for additional inspection.

Adding imputation-only variables does not control causal confounding.
MI does not establish temporal ordering or the assumptions needed to
interpret a path product causally. The choice and assessment of the
imputation model remain part of the researcher's analysis.


## Pooling convention and interval interpretation

Unstandardized indirect effects are products of Rubin-pooled path
coefficients, not averages of imputation-specific products. MC intervals
use joint multivariate normal draws with the existing manymome covariance
extraction from lavaan.mi (`scale.W = TRUE`). It inflates the within-imputation
covariance using the average relative increase in variance, incorporating
between-imputation uncertainty. This differs from the ordinary matrix sum
`W + (1 + 1/m) * B` obtained with `scale.W = FALSE`. The current interface
retains the existing manymome behavior; coverage depends on the imputation
model, covariance pooling and asymptotic approximation.
They approximate the sampling distribution asymptotically; they are not
finite-df Rubin t intervals. Small samples and high missingness require
particular care and empirical coverage checks. Standardized effects use
the existing post-fitting MI implementation.

`out$mi_info` reports the actual draw count, interval method, pooling
convention, requested/used imputations and a table of omissions with reasons.
An explicit `R` overrides the MI default. Setting both interval flags to
FALSE requests no MC draws. Explicit bootstrap requests remain unsupported.

## Customize methods and predictor relationships

The variables passed to mice are the model variables plus `mi_vars`, not
all columns of `dat`. Build named settings against those selected columns.
A named method vector is matched to the selected imputation blocks, even if
its order differs from the internally selected columns. Supply every block
name exactly once. Unnamed method vectors follow mice's positional rules.
An auxiliary variable can itself have missing values and can be a factor.
It is not added to the substantive regression equations unless included
in `cov`.

```{r}
dat$group <- factor(ifelse(dat$z > 0, "high", "low"))
dat$group[1:8] <- NA
selected <- dat[, c("x", "m", "y", "c1", "z", "group")]
methods <- mice::make.method(selected)
# Explicit choices: numeric missing mediator -> predictive mean matching;
# missing binary factor auxiliary -> logistic regression.
methods["m"] <- "pmm"
methods["group"] <- "logreg"
predictors <- mice::make.predictorMatrix(selected)
# Example restriction: group is imputed, but is not used to predict others.
# This is an illustration, not a recommended scientific restriction.
predictors[, "group"] <- 0

out_custom <- q_simple_mediation(
  x="x", m="m", y="y", cov="c1", data=dat, missing="mi",
  mi_vars=c("z", "group"),
  mice_args=list(m=5, maxit=5, method=methods, predictorMatrix=predictors),
  mi_seed=123, boot_ci=FALSE, mc_ci=FALSE, progress=FALSE
)
get_imputation(out_custom)$method
get_mi_info(out_custom)$diagnostics$auxiliary_usage
```

Columns in a predictor matrix identify predictors; rows identify target
variables (or imputation blocks). A zero column excludes a variable as a
predictor, but does not prevent that variable from being imputed. By contrast,
an empty method (`""`) disables imputation of that target. If a modeled
variable remains missing in the completed data, the quick interface rejects
it before fitting. For more advanced blocks or formulas, use mice's own
configuration tools and inspect the retained object.

## Read the diagnostics

```{r}
info <- get_mi_info(out_custom)
info$diagnostics$logged_events
info$diagnostics$unused_predictors
info$omission_reasons
imp <- get_imputation(out_custom)
# For interactive inspection, use plot(imp) to examine chain trajectories.
# Use mice::densityplot(imp) for suitable continuous variables, with enough
# imputations/iterations; judge the imputation model in its scientific context.
```

Printing the analysis reports the number of logged mice events and identifies
auxiliary variables that do not predict any actively imputed modeled variable
under the retained predictor matrix. Logged events can record constant or
collinear variables and changes to individual imputation regressions. Read
the actual event records; the absence of events does not establish convergence
or the validity of the missingness assumptions. Predictor usage is not a
measure of predictive usefulness. Active formula-based blocks make the
matrix-only diagnostic incomplete; usage indicators are then `NA`, and the
formulas should be inspected directly.

When input is a `mids` object these diagnostics remain available. A list of
completed data frames does not retain the imputation history; in that case
`get_imputation()` returns `NULL` and diagnostics have `available = FALSE`.

## Execution and reproducibility

The current MI quick workflow runs imputation, fitting and MC generation
sequentially. `parallel` and `ncores` are retained for the common quick-function
interface but do not control this MI workflow. No parallel speedup is implied.
Use `mi_seed` to control imputation and `seed` for MC generation; if `mi_seed`
is omitted the latter also controls imputation, unless `mice_args$seed` is set.
Choose only one of `mi_seed` and `mice_args$seed`.
